title: Proxy Measures and Perverse Incentives in Education
author: Doug O’Brien and Lucy Gambier
summary: Drawing on a talk at ResearchED Cornwall, the authors ask school leaders whether their targets encourage improvement of the thing they care about or create an incentive to do something nobody intended. They use Goodhart's law and a test question, how could a reasonable person improve this score without improving the goal, along with the 2012 Olympic badminton controversy as an example of perverse incentives. Cases include attendance, where a pupil leaving the roll can improve a school's percentage while home education rises, Ofsted outcomes that appear harsher for schools with more disadvantaged pupils, and Progress 8, where many schools entered whole cohorts for the ECDL qualification. Everyday examples are homework completion encouraging AI copying and CPD on mini whiteboards producing overuse. The post closes with a five-question exercise for examining one measure you currently review.
points: Once a measure becomes a target, people may raise the score without improving what it was meant to represent, and colleagues learn what attracts approval even when nobody asks.
A good test for any target is how a reasonable person could improve the score without improving the goal.
Accountability can create perverse incentives, such as a school's attendance figure improving when a persistently absent pupil leaves its roll.
Progress 8 shows how a well-designed measure can be gamed, with some schools entering whole cohorts for the ECDL qualification.
Leaders can pick one measure, write the intended outcome in plain language and ask what the number tells us, what we infer, and what colleagues expect when it looks disappointing.
quotes: Are we encouraging people to improve the thing we care about, or creating an incentive to do something we would never have intended?
People may find ways to improve the score that do little to improve the thing we hoped it represented.
A target can also be perceived. We may never ask a teacher to reduce recorded incidents. Yet colleagues can learn what appears to attract approval and what seems to invite criticism.
How could a reasonable person improve this score without improving the goal?
When a learner with very low attendance leaves its roll, the school’s future attendance percentage can improve without the barriers that learner faced having been resolved.
Many schools identified one particular qualification - The European Computer Driving Licence (ECDL) - as a way to improve their Progress 8 score. Many schools offered this to their whole cohort.
We deliver CPD on mini whiteboards, then visit lessons looking for their use. Teachers recognise what we are paying attention to and use them more frequently.
When a number improves, we should be able to explain what changed for the people it represents.
